name: Cancer Research UK: research, policy and information (charityevals, 2025-26)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: research valued as a share of the world's cancer burden (57% of the result at the defaults, spread by world population), UK tobacco policy and UK cancer information and awareness (43%).
summary: Cancer Research UK is the world's largest charitable funder of cancer research; this model covers all its charitable spending in the year to March 2026: research (£441m: grants, its own institutes and Cancer Research Horizons) and cancer information and influencing (£33m: policy campaigns and public information). Research is valued as a share of the world's cancer burden that a year of the field's research averts sooner, credited by Cancer Research UK's share of the world's cancer research funding, industry's included (about 0.6%); policy as its share of the health gain of the UK's smokefree-generation law (Tobacco and Vapes Act 2026); information as its share of the UK burden a year of everyone's cancer awareness work averts through earlier diagnosis; the deaths inside every branch's DALYs are valued by age, so mostly old deaths count less than DALYs' years lost. The result, about 0.002 years of healthy life per $1,000, is far below the site's global-health median because research results arrive after about 15 years, are shared with a field that spends some $100bn a year, cancer mortality has fallen only slowly, and the result is counted as a past average at the next dollar's share; per dollar the policy work does about twenty times as well as the research, but it is 3% of the spending. All three branches are discounted for missing data, since none has measured outcomes for Cancer Research UK's own spending; the result is dominated by judgment (how much of the burden a year of research averts, how many years sooner, Cancer Research UK's share of the field) and is mostly uncertainty.

sections.title: Cost
sections.explainer: Cancer Research UK's two charitable activities in the year to 31 March 2026, research and information and influencing, with the cost of raising the money (fundraising and trading's net loss) spread over them. From the audited accounts.

sections.title: Reach
sections.explainer: The burden the work addresses: the world's cancer for research, since a drug, test or trial result found in the UK is used worldwide; the UK's for public information and awareness; the UK's birth cohorts for the smokefree-generation law.

sections.title: Effect per unit
sections.explainer: Research: the share of the burden a year of the field's research averts once adopted, how many years sooner it comes, after the wait from funding to practice. Policy: the smokefree-generation law, the health its cohorts gain and the share of the campaign that fell in this year. Information: the share of the UK burden a year of everyone's cancer information and awareness work averts through earlier diagnosis.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Each branch has its own trust in the evidence, share of credit and missing-data step (Convention 4): Cancer Research UK's share of the world's cancer research funding for research, of everyone's resources behind the law for policy, of everyone's information and awareness work for information. The canonical rows are their DALY-weighted averages, for reading only.

sections.title: Other outcomes, in this model's unit
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for outcomes in more than one unit (docs/normalization.md 2.6): each outcome is counted in its own unit (units of value for income and deaths, WELLBYs for life satisfaction, tonnes of CO₂e, chicken pain days) and put into this model's unit by its unit's conversion over this unit's, which the headline's conversion cancels. So each moves only with its own sliders, exactly as in a model of its own unit. The rows are fixed; don't edit them.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.explainer: Years of healthy life averted by the year's research, policy and information work, per dollar.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only. The result is a past average (what a year's grants and campaigns buy, by what past research and campaigns achieved), so the next dollar is valued at Cancer Research UK's own share of it.

rows.label: Cancer research expenditure, year to 31 March 2026 (£)

source.title: Cancer Research UK, Annual report and accounts 2025/26

rows.explainer: Grants (£313.5m), Cancer Research UK's own research staff and costs in its institutes, Cancer Research Horizons and clinical trials units (£115.5m direct) and allocated support (£12.4m), as the accounts report them: new commitments, including multi-year grants, in the year. All of it is counted as cost, the royalty shares passed on to co-inventors included: the cost is what the charity spends, whatever it buys. On a cash basis it spent £416m (p. 9): basic research £88m, research on specific cancer types £185m (bowel £32m, lung £22m, brain £19m, leukaemia £18m, breast £15m and 24 more), research relevant to all cancers (infrastructure, survivorship) £87m, Cancer Research Horizons' translational work and tools £24m, administration £24m and royalty shares passed on £8m. It includes almost £8m of research at the Scotland Institute paid for by outside partners (p. 9), left in as part of the work modelled.

Policy, public affairs and campaigns in four nations against a public information service that answers about 27 million interactions a year (website, Cancer Chat, nurse helpline, roadshows, workshops; p. 6, 34-35); the activity's own description in the review leads with policy (p. 11). Our judgment: 40%, 25% to 60%. Every branch is read against the whole cost, so this sets only the per-branch figures for reading (policy_cost_gbp, info_cost_gbp) and the size of the information spending in info_attribution_share_shared's explainer, not the result.

World burden of cancer, DALYs per year (WHO GHE 2021)

source.title: WHO Global Health Estimates 2021: DALYs from malignant neoplasms (GHE cause 610), all countries, both sexes
source.url: https://xmart-api-public.who.int/DEX_CMS/GHE_FULL?$filter=DIM_GHECAUSE_CODE eq 610 and DIM_YEAR_CODE eq 2021 and DIM_SEX_CODE eq 'TOTAL'
source.note: Sum over 183 countries, 2021, all ages: 254,522,509 DALYs (YLL plus YLD) from malignant neoplasms.
source.cell: every country, DIM_AGEGROUP_CODE TOTAL, VAL_DALY_COUNT_NUMERIC, summed

rows.explainer: Cancer worldwide, WHO's 2021 estimates: 255 million DALYs a year, the same source as the age split of the deaths (facts: death_ages, cancer_*). GBD's estimate is similar (about 250 to 270 million); the range covers both and their uncertainty. The whole world, because Cancer Research UK's results (drugs such as temozolomide and abiraterone, trial results, screening evidence) are used wherever such advances reach; uptake outside rich countries is lower, and that is in the share averted, not here.

rows.label: Information: UK burden of cancer, DALYs per year (WHO GHE 2021)

source.title: WHO Global Health Estimates 2021: DALYs from malignant neoplasms (GHE cause 610), United Kingdom, both sexes
source.url: https://xmart-api-public.who.int/DEX_CMS/GHE_FULL?$filter=DIM_GHECAUSE_CODE eq 610 and DIM_YEAR_CODE eq 2021 and DIM_SEX_CODE eq 'TOTAL'
source.note: United Kingdom, 2021, all ages: 3,681,626 DALYs (uncertainty interval 3,277,448 to 4,085,805).

rows.explainer: The burden the public information and awareness work addresses: cancer in the UK, where the service runs. WHO's own uncertainty interval as the range.

rows.label: Share of the burden the advances from one year of the field's research avert each year once in use
rows.explainer: One judgment, the product of how much of the burden the kind of advances funded address and the chance a year's portfolio delivers one (split below for reading); worked as for cardiovascular research in british-heart-foundation-charityevals, on cancer's own record. The US cancer death rate fell 34% from 1991 to 2022, about 1.3% a year, from less smoking, earlier detection and better treatment (Siegel et al., Cancer statistics 2025). About half of that is earlier detection and treatment, the rest mostly smoking (our judgment: the American Cancer Society names the three causes without splitting them): so research advances avert about 0.6% of a rich country's burden a year. High-income countries carry 23% of the world's cancer DALYs (59.7 of 254.5 million, WHO GHE 2021), so about 0.14% of the world burden, plus a lower rate in the rest of the world where uptake is low (a quarter of it on 77%: another 0.12%). Part of that is uptake of older advances rather than the year's new research: about half. So a year of the world's research averts about 0.13% of the burden, 0.03% to 0.5%: less than cardiovascular research's 0.3%, since cancer mortality has fallen more slowly than heart disease.

rows.label: Share of that burden the advances from a year of the field's research avert once adopted
rows.explainer: For reading: the share of the burden the kind of advances funded (a new drug class, a test, a screening programme) address at the uptake they reach, a few percent each (HPV vaccination for cervical cancer, targeted therapies in their cancers, bowel screening). The result reads only its product with p_success (share_burden_averted_per_research_year), so this split doesn't add a second range.

rows.label: Implied probability a year's portfolio of the field turns into such an advance in practice (for reading)
rows.explainer: The judged product over the judged share addressed: about 3%. For comparison, about 1 in 3 cancer drugs entering phase 3 and about 1 in 30 from phase 1 reach approval (Wong, Siah and Lo, Biostatistics 2019, oncology the lowest of any area); Cancer Research UK's portfolio is mostly basic and translational science.

rows.label: Years sooner the advance arrives because the field is funded this year
rows.explainer: Without a year of funding, the same advances would come later from the following years' research, industry and other countries; this is how much later. Its credit is split by Cancer Research UK's share of the field's funding (research_attribution_share_shared), and it already answers "would it have happened anyway" (Convention 5), so there is no counterfactual adjustment as well. 5 years, 2 to 15, as for cardiovascular research (british-heart-foundation-charityevals); checked against the returns-to-research reference class below (ref_dalys_per_gbp against research_dalys_per_gbp_credited).

rows.label: Years from the funding until the result is in practice

source.title: Glover et al. (2014), BMC Medicine 12:99 (Europe PMC full text)
source.quote: Calculation of the IRR incorporated an estimated elapsed time of 15 years.

rows.explainer: The lag the UK study of cancer research found between research spending and health benefit; cardiovascular research had about 17 years, and screening and guideline work is quicker (Morris, Wooding and Grant 2011), new drugs slower. Discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Discount for the wait until the result is in practice
rows.explainer: The wait discounted at the shared rate.

Research: value of a cancer death at 70 or older (world, units of value)
rows.explainer: GiveWell's five-year weights for 70–74 and 75–79 (their mean) and for 80 and over (80–84; 85 and over has the same weight), mixed by the share of these deaths at 80 or older.

rows.label: Research: value of a death averted (units of value)
rows.explainer: Every death the site counts is valued by the age it happens at (docs/normalization.md, decision 2026-10-31 #4): GiveWell's moral weights by age over the ages of cancer deaths worldwide, 47% of them at 70 or older and 41% at 50 to 69 (WHO GHE 2021, facts: death_ages), 50–69 at the 50–74 band and 70 and over at the five-year weights for 70–79 and 80 and over (references: families/high-income-care.md), times the value-of-a-life slider.

rows.label: Research: deaths per DALY
rows.explainer: The burden is WHO's DALYs, mostly years of life lost to deaths at WHO's reference life expectancy, which the value-of-a-life slider wouldn't touch. As everywhere on the site, each DALY is split into its illness part, kept as DALYs, and the deaths behind the rest, valued by age in units of value and brought into healthy years by the bridge (docs/normalization.md, decision 2026-10-31 #4, and 2.6).

rows.label: Research: share of each DALY that is illness, not death
rows.explainer: Kept as healthy years; the rest of each DALY is deaths (the row above).

rows.label: Expected DALYs averted by the year's research of the whole field (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: Healthy years averted by the year's research of the whole field, in WHO's DALYs (deaths split out below).

rows.label: Reference class: health-gain return on UK cancer research (internal rate of return)

source.title: Glover et al. (2014), BMC Medicine 12:99 (Europe PMC full text)
source.quote: This produced a best-estimate IRR of 10%, compared with 9% previously estimated for cardiovascular disease research.

rows.explainer: Context, for reading only (not on the result's path): the sanity bound of references/families/medical-research.md, UK public and charity cancer research's return in UK health gains, 10% a year; cardiovascular research's 9% is the low end.

rows.label: Reference class: lag from research spending to health gain
rows.explainer: The same 15-year lag as the chain.

rows.label: Reference class: the study's value of a QALY (£)

source.title: Glover et al. (2014), BMC Medicine 12:99 (Europe PMC full text)
source.quote: (using a base-case value of a QALY of GB£25,000)

rows.explainer: Context, for reading only (not on the result's path): the study's own conversion from health to money, used only to turn its return back into QALYs for the check; it moves nothing on the result's path.

rows.label: Reference class: UK healthy years per £ of research the return implies (for reading)
rows.explainer: A 10% return with a 15-year lag means each £ buys a stream of about £0.42 of UK health a year from year 15 on; at £25,000 a QALY and the shared discount rate that is about 0.00023 healthy years per £, in the UK alone, with UK research credited with 17% of UK gains (Glover et al.).

rows.label: The chain's healthy years per £ of Cancer Research UK research, after its adjustments (for reading)
rows.explainer: In WHO's DALYs, before the deaths are valued by age, so in the reference's own units. Against ref_dalys_per_gbp: the chain gives about a thirtieth of it (0.000008 against 0.00023). The two count different things: the reference credits UK research with 17% of UK gains, far above the UK's few percent of the world's cancer research funding, while the chain credits Cancer Research UK its funding share of world gains. The gap is wider than for cardiovascular research (where the chain is about half the reference, british-heart-foundation-charityevals) because the world spends several times as much on cancer research as on cardiovascular research for a burden 40% smaller, and cancer mortality has fallen more slowly, so each pound of cancer research buys less; the UK study's 10% is a UK-only best case that credits research with gains (screening programmes, care) that also took other spending. We take the chain as the best guess; with years_brought_forward, share_burden_averted_per_research_year and research_attribution_share_shared all at their high ends it reaches about two-thirds of the reference.

source.title: DHSC, Tobacco and Vapes Bill impact assessment (March 2024; superseded by the November 2024 assessment of the reintroduced bill)
source.quote: The population of those aged 14 to 30 is 11,777,381

rows.explainer: The age group the impact assessment models the law's effect on smoking uptake in, from ONS 2021 mid-year estimates; with the number of single years of age it gives one year's cohort.

rows.label: Advocacy: single years of age from 14 to 30

source.title: DHSC, Tobacco and Vapes Bill impact assessment (March 2024; superseded by the November 2024 assessment of the reintroduced bill)
source.quote: The population of those aged 14 to 30 is 11,777,381

rows.explainer: Ages 14 to 30 inclusive are 17 single years, so the band divided by 17 is an average cohort.

rows.label: Advocacy: UK population ÷ England's

source.title: DHSC, Tobacco and Vapes Bill impact assessment (March 2024; superseded by the November 2024 assessment of the reintroduced bill)
source.quote: all the England estimates have been uplifted by 1.19 to provide estimates for the costs and benefits of the smokefree generation policy to the UK.

rows.explainer: The Act covers the whole UK; the impact assessment scales England by population, and so do we.

rows.label: Advocacy: people per year brought under the smokefree-generation law (one UK birth cohort)
rows.explainer: The Tobacco and Vapes Act (Royal Assent April 2026) bans the sale of tobacco to anyone born on or after 1 January 2009. Each year the law is brought forward covers one more birth cohort, about 820,000 people in the UK; so the yearly flow the win counts is one cohort, and $win_years_counted counts the years.

rows.label: Advocacy: share of a covered cohort kept from smoking
rows.explainer: The impact assessment's central scenario (a 30% fall in the yearly rate of taking up smoking below the age of sale, picked with tobacco-control experts (19 consulted, 14 replied) and chosen over stronger scenarios to allow for underage sales and proxy purchases, paras 154-161) takes smoking among 14 to 30 year olds from 9.2% in the baseline to effectively zero, "9.2 percentage points lower in 2056" (para. 169). That is the high end. Our best guess, 8 points, takes a little off for a baseline already falling faster than the assessment's flat steady state (a criticism made to the Public Bill Committee); leakage is not taken off again here or in adv_evidence_adj. The low end, 2.5 points, is the assessment's weakest scenario (Scenario 5, 6.7% against 9.2%, Table 27). The figures are from the March 2024 impact assessment; the November 2024 one for the reintroduced bill keeps the same smokefree-generation modelling.

rows.label: Advocacy: lifetime DALYs lost per person who smokes as a young adult
rows.explainer: Doll et al.'s 50-year follow-up of British doctors (BMJ 2004): lifelong smokers die about 10 years sooner, and stopping at 30 avoids almost all of that, at 40 most of it. Many young smokers stop, so a person smoking at 14 to 30 loses a few healthy years on average, deaths and illness from heart disease, cancer and lung disease together. Check against the impact assessment: with the rest of the branch a covered UK cohort gains about 198,000 DALYs undiscounted (824,000 × 8% × 3), about 109,000 at the government's 1.5% over 40 years; the assessment's own figure, deaths only and only those before 2100, is about 950,000 QALYs in present value (£66.7bn at £70,000) over all the cohorts it covers, most of whose smoking deaths fall after 2100, so roughly nine cohorts' worth by our figure. Consistent within the range.

rows.label: Advocacy: years from the law biting on a cohort until its health gains
rows.explainer: Smoking kills and disables mostly in middle and old age: the impact assessment finds "no health benefits would be expected until 2044" (para. 178), 17 years after the law starts, with gains rising to 2100. A cohort kept from smoking at 18 has its gains mostly at 50 to 80, about 40 years later. Discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Advocacy: DALYs averted per person in a covered cohort (lifetime, discounted to the law's start)
rows.explainer: The share kept from smoking times the healthy years a young smoker loses, discounted over the decades until those years come. Per cohort member, so multiplied by one cohort per year counted.

rows.label: Policy: value of a smoking death at 70 or older (UK, units of value)
rows.explainer: GiveWell's five-year weights for 70–79 and for 80 and over, mixed by the share of these deaths at 80 or older.

rows.label: Policy: value of a death averted (units of value)
rows.explainer: Every death the site counts is valued by the age it happens at (docs/normalization.md, decision 2026-10-31 #4): GiveWell's moral weights by age over the ages of smoking deaths in the UK, two thirds of them at 70 or older (GBD 2023, facts: death_ages), 50–69 at the 50–74 band and 70 and over at the five-year weights for 70–79 and 80 and over (references: families/high-income-care.md), times the value-of-a-life slider.

rows.explainer: The burden is GBD DALYs, mostly years of life lost to deaths at GBD's life expectancy, which the value-of-a-life slider wouldn't touch. As everywhere on the site, each DALY is split into its illness part, kept as DALYs, and the deaths behind the rest, valued by age in units of value and brought into healthy years by the bridge (docs/normalization.md, decision 2026-10-31 #4, and 2.6).

rows.label: Policy: share of each DALY that is illness, not death
rows.explainer: Kept as healthy years; the rest of each DALY is deaths (the row above).

rows.label: Advocacy: share of all the campaigning behind the law done in this year
rows.explainer: The law is won (Royal Assent April 2026, three weeks after the year ends), so the question is how much of the win this year's work bought. The bill was introduced in November 2024 and spent this year in the House of Lords, the last stretch of a campaign that ran from the 2023 plan (and of decades of tobacco-control work before it); Cancer Research UK's share of the people and money behind it is in adv_attribution_share_shared. A fifth, from about four years of active campaigning with the final year weighing more. The same figure as in british-heart-foundation-charityevals: the two charities' years are the same (to 31 March 2026).

rows.label: Advocacy: years a won reform counts
rows.explainer: The site's one answer (docs/normalization.md 2.9).

rows.label: Advocacy: years from the year modelled until the law takes effect
rows.explainer: The sale ban starts on 1 January 2027 (the impact assessment's appraisal starts on that date), about a year after the middle of the year modelled. The longer wait until the health gains is in adv_dalys_per_person_year.

rows.label: Advocacy: discounted years of impact
Expected DALYs averted by advocacy (before adjustments)
Information: share of the UK cancer burden a year of everyone's cancer information and awareness work averts
rows.explainer: What a year of public cancer information and awareness (NHS campaigns, charities' websites, helplines and roadshows) does: people who know the signs and their screening invitations present earlier, and earlier stage means better survival. Anchor: the national Be Clear on Cancer lung campaign of 2012 raised the share of non-small-cell lung cancers diagnosed at stage I by 3.1 percentage points and resections by 2.3 points among patients seen during the campaign (Ironmonger et al., Br J Cancer 2015): a few hundred more people operated on, perhaps 100 deaths delayed by years, about 1,000 healthy years, 0.03% of the UK's cancer burden from one national campaign. A year of all such work, several campaigns' worth across cancers plus the standing information services, about 0.1%, 0.02% to 0.4%. Risk reduction (stopping smoking, diet) adds a little more; the evidence is weak, which the range and info_evidence_adj carry.

rows.label: Information: years from the year's work until the deaths are averted
rows.explainer: Earlier diagnosis happens within months; the deaths it averts or delays come over the following years (most cancer deaths within five years of diagnosis). Two years, 1 to 5. Discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Information: deaths per DALY

As everywhere on the site, each DALY is split into its illness part, kept as DALYs, and the deaths behind the rest, valued by age in units of value and brought into healthy years by the bridge (docs/normalization.md, decision 2026-10-31 #4, and 2.6).

rows.label: Information: share of each DALY that is illness, not death
rows.explainer: Kept as healthy years; the rest of each DALY is deaths (the row above).

rows.label: Information: DALYs averted by a year of everyone's information and awareness work (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: A year's work against a year's cost (a flow, Convention 3): the burden it averts, after the wait, before Cancer Research UK's share.

rows.label: Research: evidence adjustment, a multiplier
rows.explainer: The research chain rests on judgments calibrated to the record of cancer mortality and to returns-to-research studies, which their authors call best-case estimates (they credit research with gains that also came from changes in behaviour and care). 0.7, as for cardiovascular research in british-heart-foundation-charityevals; the range runs to face value.

rows.label: Research: Cancer Research UK's share of the world's cancer research funding
rows.explainer: The years brought forward are the whole field's, so Cancer Research UK is credited with its share of all funders' spending on it (about $580m of research a year). Non-commercial funders: the US National Cancer Institute alone had a $7.2bn appropriation in 2024 (NCI fact book), and other US institutes, the Department of Defense and US charities add more; UK public and charity cancer research was about £850m a year by 2009 (Glover et al.), of which Cancer Research UK is about half; Europe's other public and charity funders, Japan, China, Canada and Australia add several billion: about $16bn a year. Industry, counted in full: the industry spent about $288bn on R&D in 2024 (Evaluate Pharma, via BioSpace), and cancer is its largest area, 38% of industry-sponsored phase I to III trial starts in 2025 (IQVIA, Global Trends in R&D 2026). Its share of spending is our judgment against that share of trial starts: about 30%, 25% to 38% (early-phase cancer trials are many and small; late ones are long): some $85bn. All funders together spend about $100bn a year on cancer research, of which Cancer Research UK is about 0.6%. Those anchors alone give 0.46% to 0.98% (industry at 38% or 25%); the range is wider, 0.3% to 1.2%, for what they leave out or may overstate: diagnostics and medical-device R&D outside the pharmaceutical total and China's public funding (lower), and the non-commercial total, which is rough (higher). british-heart-foundation-charityevals counts industry the same way, at cardiovascular's share of the industry's R&D.

rows.label: Advocacy: evidence adjustment, a multiplier
rows.explainer: The effect of a generational sale ban is modelled, not observed (New Zealand repealed its own before it took effect); underage sales and leakage are already in the assessment's central scenario and adv_prevalence_cut, so this covers the rest: substitution by vaping (which the same Act regulates) and the chance of later repeal. 0.7, as the research branch.

rows.label: Policy: Cancer Research UK's share of everyone's resources behind the law
rows.explainer: The government proposed and drafted the law, Parliament passed it, and many groups campaigned (Action on Smoking and Health, Cancer Research UK, the British Heart Foundation, the royal colleges, directors of public health). Cancer Research UK ran its Smokefree UK campaign through the bill's passage in all four UK parliaments (mobile billboards, supporters' letters to MPs; annual report p. 28), funds much of the research the case rested on, and part-funds ASH. Government staff time counts among the resources (Convention 2). One in ten, twice the British Heart Foundation's 5% in british-heart-foundation-charityevals, since smoking is the leading cause of cancer and tobacco control is a long-standing core campaign of Cancer Research UK's, with a larger policy budget; 5% to 20%.

rows.label: Information: evidence adjustment, a multiplier
rows.explainer: Awareness campaigns' effects come from before-and-after comparisons, not trials, and part of the extra diagnoses are overdiagnosis or would have come months later anyway; a standing information service's effect is less studied than a campaign's. 0.6, below research's 0.7, as for the British Heart Foundation's implementation pilots (also a chain of judgments without trials); 0.3 to 0.9.

rows.label: Information: Cancer Research UK's share of everyone's resources on UK cancer information and awareness
rows.explainer: Cancer Research UK spends about £20m a year on public information and awareness (info_cost_gbp). Others: the NHS (its website, national awareness campaigns and screening invitations), Macmillan Cancer Support's information and support (several times larger), the disease charities and GPs' own advice. One in five, 10% to 40%.

rows.label: Research: missing-data step
rows.explainer: Thin: the chain is our judgment calibrated on the record of cancer mortality and returns-to-research studies; no measure of what Cancer Research UK's own grants achieved exists. So the shared missing-data step applies (templates.md Convention 12).

rows.label: Policy: missing-data step
rows.explainer: Thin: the law's health effect comes from the government's impact assessment (modelled, not observed) and Cancer Research UK's part in it is our judgment. So the shared missing-data step applies (templates.md Convention 12).

rows.label: Information: missing-data step
rows.explainer: Thin: no measure of what Cancer Research UK's information services do to diagnosis or deaths exists; the effect is our judgment from campaign evaluations. So the shared missing-data step applies (templates.md Convention 12).

rows.label: Research: share that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: 1: the years brought forward already say how much later the advance would have come without the year's funding (Convention 5).

rows.label: Policy: share that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: 1: $win_years_counted already says how much later the law would have come without the campaign (Convention 5).

rows.label: Information: share that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: 1: info_share_burden_averted is already the gain over a year without the work (people who would have presented in time anyway are not in it), and others' work is in the attribution share (Convention 5).

rows.label: Research: Cancer Research UK's share of the credit
rows.explainer: Cancer Research UK's share of the resources behind this branch's outcome; it applies whichever way credit is shared.

rows.label: Policy: Cancer Research UK's share of the credit
rows.explainer: Cancer Research UK's share of the resources behind this branch's outcome; it applies whichever way credit is shared.

rows.explainer: Cancer Research UK's share of the field's funding for research, of the campaign's resources for policy and of everyone's information and awareness work: the DALY-weighted average of the branches, for reading only; each branch applies its own.

rows.label: Share of credit used

rows.explainer: The DALY-weighted average of the branches, for reading only: each branch applies its own share (research_, adv_, info_attribution_share).

rows.label: Evidence adjustment (outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)

rows.explainer: The DALY-weighted average of the branches' trust in their evidence, for reading only; each branch applies its own.

rows.label: Missing-data step (DALY-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)

rows.label: Share of the outcome that wouldn't have happened anyway

rows.explainer: The DALY-weighted average of the branches, for reading only: 1 in every branch (research_, adv_, info_counterfactual_adj), since the years brought forward, the years a won law counts and the share averted against no work already say what would have happened anyway (Convention 5).

rows.label: All adjustments combined
rows.formula: (research_dalys * research_total_adj + advocacy_dalys * adv_total_adj + info_dalys * info_total_adj) / (research_dalys + advocacy_dalys + info_dalys)
rows.explainer: The DALY-weighted average of the branches' products of adjustments (research_, adv_, info_total_adj), for reading only; each branch applies its own.

rows.label: Benefits and harms not modelled, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Benefits not counted: the Act's limits on youth vaping and second-hand smoke averted (both left out by the impact assessment's health figures); Cancer Research UK's other policy wins this year, the restrictions on junk-food advertising and promotions that came into force (obesity is a risk factor for 13 cancers) and the National Cancer Plan for England with its targeted lung screening and earlier-diagnosis commitments (largely announced before, so a small part of their value); the research workforce, institutes and tools that later research uses; the start-ups Cancer Research Horizons forms (99 so far, £3.5bn raised), whose private money is not counted as a gain. Harms: research effort drawn from other diseases, and the overdiagnosis that awareness work brings beyond what info_evidence_adj takes off. Positive on balance: 10%, -5% to 30% (the British Heart Foundation's model has 8% for a smaller set of other policy wins).

rows.explainer: Each branch's illness with its own adjustments, plus the deaths through the bridge (already adjusted branch by branch, Convention 4), times the unmodelled share.

Cancer Research UK's own staff pay as a share of the cost modelled

source.title: Cancer Research UK, Annual report and accounts 2025/26, note 9 employees

rows.explainer: Cancer Research UK's own staff over the full cost modelled (Convention 1). The group's staff cost £201.2m (wages, social security, pensions, note 9) for an average 5,108 people: 1,228 in charitable activities (including the scientists of its own institutes), 637 in support services and 3,243 in fundraising and trading. Trading's staff are paid by trading, whose net result alone is in the cost, so they are left out: about two thirds of the 3,243 work in the shops, at below-average pay. Charitable and support staff at the average pay, about £73m, plus fundraising staff, about £40m, is about £115m of £615m: 19%, 14% to 25%. The researchers the grants pay are university staff, whose pay is the grants' cost, not Cancer Research UK staff's forgone salary.

rows.label: Pay gap versus comparable jobs elsewhere
rows.explainer: Cancer Research UK's staff are UK charity staff (its own scientists, grant managers, policy, information and support staff): the shared gap for UK charities.
